story: You give your opponents creatures which make their game worse and they’re forced to keep them. That’s the whole hook. Steel Golem shuts off their creature plays. Grid Monitor does the same. Flesh Reaver chunks their life every time they use it. Then you pass something like Archfiend of the Dross across the table and they’re suddenly on a clock they didn’t ask for. Tick, tick… you lose.
You’re not necessarily attacking or committing much to the board. Somehow, everyone else is taking damage, missing plays, or stuck managing something you handed them.
You don’t rush this deck. Set up, draw, make land drops, maybe keep Phyrexian Arena ticking along. Then Jon lands, and from that point on every creature has a destination.

Switcheroo, Shifting Loyalties and Modify Memory mean nothing stays solved. Assault Suit and Grafted Wargear make combat decisions awkward after the handoff. Crystal Shard lets you pull something back and send it somewhere worse.
You’re not closing the game yourself. You’re making sure nobody else gets to play well enough to close it either.

story: This deck plays with a soft political posture that keeps early pressure off while it develops a board that can rapidly annihilate.

Kwain allows each player to draw a card and gain a life, which naturally lowers tension and encourages momentum. It doesn’t announce itself as the primary threat. Instead, that sly generosity buys time to assemble pieces quietly.

At its core, this is a hare-apparent deck. If left alone to develop it can get out of hand quickly. The commander’s political edge helps blur threat assessment just long enough to establish position. The early turns feel cooperative; the midgame layers presence without overextending; then the board is suddenly overrun with rabbits.

This deck was stress-tested extensively over a few months. In one session, Caleb and Lilly put Josh and Luke through their paces. Even with Luke using his signature XL deck, Caleb and Lilly decimated Josh and Luke. Caleb said, “I wanted to play every card, it was sick.”
The Covert Builder plays beneath the surface, manages threat perception, and accelerates only once protection and position are secured.

story: This deck plays with a quiet, reactive playstyle that allows you to play the top card of your library if it has flash or flying. It doesn’t explode onto the board or obviously declare itself the threat. Instead, it develops patiently while holding mana open and advancing at instant speed during opponents’ turns.
A land drop and a passed turn is often all it needs to stay on a winning trajectory. Over time, the incremental advantage compounds and opponents realise they’re playing into your timing, not theirs.

This deck suits players who value position over spectacle. You spend early turns observing, absorbing information, and choosing precise moments to respond. Once the game develops, open mana represents real consequences. This is disciplined control that tightens as the game goes on.
The Flash Architect plays for control of tempo and information rather than raw speed. It wins by leveraging timing, discouraging overextension, and closing once opponents are stretched thin.
